findings.passage: What makes it more than that is that the rule holds across both choices, including the one that made his own party furious.
findings.problem: The cross-decision consistency is the author's construction, not his. The only stated rule (S08, Aug. 2025) concerns redistricting: on-schedule 2021 maps did not justify a quorum break, mid-decade maps do. His stated reason for the 2021 return was pragmatic, not that rule: 'Given this success and recognizing that we can't break quorum indefinitely, some of my fellow quorum breakers and I returned' (S07 op-ed, Aug. 27, 2021; reopened on sacurrent.com). The 2021 walkout itself was against an on-schedule voting bill, which the 2025 on-schedule/mid-decade distinction would not obviously license. So 'each time by a rule he can state' and, in 'Why One still beats Three', 'The quorum line held across two opposite decisions' overstate a sourced consistency and are used as discriminating evidence for Type 1.
findings.acceptance_test: The article gives the 2021 rationale in his own words (success achieved, quorum break unsustainable, harm reduction) and either (a) drops the claim that one rule governs both decisions or (b) cites a sourced statement in which he applies the same principle to both. 'The quorum line held across two opposite decisions' is removed from the discriminator paragraph or rewritten so that it doesn't claim a consistency the sources don't show. Evidence claim C09's inference is updated to match.

findings.passage: By 2025 he held a safe seat and was weighing a Senate run, so leaving was rewarded, and a rule stated after the fact can be messaging.
findings.problem: The article never says how he got the safe seat. Per Wikipedia (S09), after 2021 redistricting made his swing HD-52 significantly more Republican, he ran in 2022 in neighboring HD-50, a safe Democratic seat vacated by Celia Israel (won the primary with 78.5%). That was a self-protective career move in the same window as the seminary decision, and it bears directly on the thesis that his central fear is 'self-preservation' ('when people hang on to these positions or are trying to reach for the next position, then everything becomes about self-preservation', S01-presidency). He also made that statement while running for a higher office. The draft leaves both points unconfronted while counting the term-limit pledge as a key One discriminator.
findings.acceptance_test: The article states the 2022 move from HD-52 to HD-50 with its date and source and weighs it in the Type 3 case or the discriminator section. The passage quoting 'trying to reach for the next position' acknowledges that he said it while seeking a higher office. A claim entry covers the move.

findings.passage: The Three evidence, the class size, the super PAC and the repositioning, all arrives under the heaviest statewide pressure, when almost anyone adapts, so it discriminates less than the earlier choices.
findings.problem: The discount is applied to one side only. Much of the One evidence comes from the same high-incentive period: the Rogan push-back (July 2025, weeks before his Senate launch), the Bartlett 'No' to a presidential run, the two-term pledge and the 'including me' line (all Sept. 2026, two months before an election he was favored to win, with 2028 speculation already public, per the S01-presidency context). The draft calls the Rogan exchange 'The clearest live test.' If late evidence is weak because 'almost anyone adapts,' disavowing ambition and pre-committing to term limits are equally adaptive campaign behavior. The early One evidence is also weaker than presented. He returned with a group of Democrats (S07 names four), the return suited his swing district (acknowledged), and he was named a Texas Monthly Top 10 Best Legislator at the end of that session (S09), so elite reputation partly offset the cost.
findings.acceptance_test: The article applies the same incentive discount to both sides. Either the 2025–2026 One evidence (C11, C12, C62, C64) is explicitly weighted as campaign-period statements, or the article explains why it survives the discount that the late Three evidence fails. The 'clearest live test' label is earned or removed. The confidence statement reflects what remains of the early record (the 2021 return and seminary) after that adjustment.

findings.passage: Seminary later became central to his political brand, but nobody could have banked on that in 2021.
findings.problem: This sentence is unsupported speculation, and it rests on a choice the draft calls costly without showing a cost. He enrolled while keeping his seat, won reelection (to a safer seat, see critic-02), and lost no advancement. By March 2021 he was already doing faith-forward political commentary on the Activist Theology podcast (S18), and in 2021 he made the 'God is nonbinary' remark on the House floor (S17), so a faith-based political identity predated seminary. 'A Three who doubts his impact usually looks for a role where the impact is more visible' is an unsourced generalization doing discriminating work. The FAQ repeats the overclaim: 'his costliest choices ran against image and advancement ... went to seminary after doubting his impact'.
findings.acceptance_test: 'nobody could have banked on that in 2021' is deleted or supported by a source. The seminary choice is described as what it was (part-time study while remaining in office) and not counted as a costly choice against advancement unless a specific cost is sourced. The FAQ 'Why isn't James Talarico read as a Type 3?' no longer lists seminary among choices that 'ran against image and advancement' without that support.

findings.passage: A Three's nightmare is failing or being unseen. The one Talarico keeps describing is becoming the thing he fights, and he builds a rule in advance to stop himself.
findings.problem: 'Keeps describing' implies a fear repeated across occasions, but the evidence (C11, C63, C64) comes from one interview (Bartlett, Sept. 2026). The 'including me' line was his answer to 'how are you different from other politicians?', a campaign-pitch question he redirected to 'the system' (S01-system context). The two-term pledge is also a platform plank: he proposes term limits for all of Congress (S09). So 'builds a rule in advance to stop himself' reads a policy position as a private pre-commitment.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage either cites a second dated occasion, independent of the Bartlett interview, where he expresses the fear of his own corruption, or says the statement comes from one September 2026 interview. It notes that the self-imposed limit matches his general congressional term-limits platform.

findings.passage: In his telling, his aggression always arrives with a license: he is protecting someone and correcting a wrong.
findings.problem: The adverse record is softened. The article presents the Paxton attack through the 'love requires accountability' gloss he gave months later on a podcast. It leaves out the contemporaneous act reported in the same Texas Monthly source (S17): on runoff night he posted Paxton's mugshot alongside 'the most corrupt politician in America.' That was attention-seeking aggression with no protective framing at the time. 'Always' is also a universal the record doesn't support, and the article's own unresolved 'mediocre' episode cuts against it.
findings.acceptance_test: The Paxton section reports the mugshot post with date and source next to the later 'love requires accountability' explanation. 'Always' is qualified (for example, 'in his retellings'), or the article acknowledges contemporaneous instances where the license is supplied only afterward.

findings.passage: The One reading predicts he keeps the two-term pledge and keeps saying no to the next position. The Three reading predicts both soften in the spotlight.
findings.problem: The closing test doesn't discriminate. Breaking a high-profile public pledge is image-costly, so an image-protective Three would also keep it. 'Keeps saying no to the next position' sits awkwardly beside the fact that he just took a higher office. The ending presents as a decisive test something both readings predict, which overstates how falsifiable the thesis is.
findings.acceptance_test: The closing names at least one future observable that the two readings predict differently, such as whether he corrects a favorable but inaccurate story without being challenged, or keeps a principle when keeping it costs a visible win. Otherwise it states plainly that pledge-keeping is consistent with both types.

findings.passage: James Talarico walked back into a walkout under fire and capped his own Senate
findings.problem: The metadata description gets the key fact backwards. He returned to the House floor, leaving the 2021 walkout early. 'Walked back into a walkout' reads as rejoining it. Search snippets will show this sentence.
findings.acceptance_test: The description says he returned early from (left) the 2021 walkout under fire from his own party, stays within 120–170 characters, and agrees with the body.

protected_passages.passage: He names the price himself: the applause and the money. But the same Tribune report notes he then held a competitive suburban seat and had drawn two serious Republican challengers. Going back to work was also good politics.
protected_passages.reason: It confronts the self-interest explanation in the same breath as the flattering quote, which is the honesty the article needs everywhere.

protected_passages.passage: The Daily Wire's headline called his whole origin story a lie, which the reporting does not show. It does show a story told bigger than the documents.
protected_passages.reason: It is fair in both directions: it rejects a partisan overstatement without excusing the documented inflation.

protected_passages.passage: It does not explain the 45 students. A man whose stated fear is his own corruption told a classroom story bigger than the records, and his campaign reframed it instead of conceding. A One can talk himself into a story being true in spirit. That is still a dent, not a footnote.
protected_passages.reason: Adverse evidence is left standing against the leading type instead of being explained away.

protected_passages.passage: Bernal is a friendly witness, and wanting to do more also fits a helper or an achiever.
protected_passages.reason: It labels the witness's interest and names the alternatives right next to the most quotable testimony.

protected_passages.passage: Theft, sickness, corruption: the words come easily to him. Ones usually mean them. So do good preachers.
protected_passages.reason: A distinctive, compact statement of the learned-register alternative that the type argument can't rule out.

assessment: The draft is unusually willing to state adverse evidence (the swing-district incentive, the 45-student records, the super PAC, the general-election repositioning, the unresolved 'mediocre' account), and its handling of the Daily Wire overstatement is fair. Its weakness is in the causal stories that carry the Type 1 verdict. The 'one rule across both quorum decisions' story is assembled by the author and contradicted by his own 2021 rationale. Seminary is counted as a costly choice without a demonstrated cost. Late-campaign statements that favor Type 1 escape the incentive discount applied to late evidence that favors Type 3. The 2022 move from a swing seat to a safe seat, which bears directly on the 'self-preservation' fear he names, is omitted. Once these are corrected, the early costly-choice record is thinner than presented. Medium confidence may survive, but the discriminator paragraph should rest on evidence that holds up under symmetric scrutiny. Similarity leads were checked. The 1.0 match with daniela-amodei is the stock body-triad orientation sentence (ordinary type vocabulary), and the 0.51 match is the shared 'Ones are driven by a need to be good' answer formula. The actual arguments are specific to Talarico, so I did not report reuse as a finding. Risk flags carried forward: sensitive_allegations (the 'mediocre' remark) and contested_typing (3 vs 1, with 9 and 2 tested). The 2021 op-ed context (S07) and Wikipedia's district and legislative history (S09) were reopened for this review.
